articles.title: Your Agents are Only as Good as Your Data Context
articles.description: Agents get only data points, so a sales spike from a limited-time promotion reads to them as a lasting trend worth producing more stock for. A semantic layer supplies the missing translation, defining what each column and event means in the words teams actually use in Slack and meetings. Amplitude's own layer took its agent to correct answers 80 to 90 percent of the time, with custom instructions closing the rest.
articles.one-liner: AI agents frequently misinterpret data spikes as trends, necessitating a semantic layer that defines metrics using human business terminology.

summary.what: Amplitude’s Michele Morales explains that agents require a semantic layer—mapping database columns to Slack-friendly, plain-language business definitions—to prevent incorrect analysis. Amplitude reports that building this context improved their own agent's accuracy to 80-90%.
summary.why: The gap between raw database schemas and business reality is the primary failure point for AI agents. Success depends on moving from raw data feeds to curated context.
summary.takeaway: Start building your semantic layer by drafting definitions using your team's internal terminology, then use AI to refine those drafts against existing DB metadata.

articles.deep-summary:
* Use plain language definitions for all data columns to avoid ambiguity.
* Maintain a centralized list of synonyms and labels to match user queries.
* Flag deprecated fields, duplicates, and untrusted data points.
* Map data lineage to understand downstream impacts.
* Provide agents with 'certified' datasets for specific questions to reduce hallucination.
* Use AI to draft the initial definitions, then have human subject matter experts verify them.
* Implement feedback loops where incorrect agent answers trigger further context refinement.
articles.decoder:
* **Semantic layer**: A business-facing representation of data that defines relationships, metrics, and terminology so both humans and AI understand the context of data fields.
* **Data lineage**: The lifecycle of data that includes its origins and where it moves over time.
* **Agent traces**: Logs of an AI agent's reasoning process and function calls, used for debugging performance.

articles.title: Accordion Icons: Which Ones Work Best?
articles.description: NN/g research finds real differences between carets, arrows, and plus icons on accordions, with the caret the safest choice and the most tapped. With no icon at all, users expect the item to open a new page. Split menus, where label and icon trigger different actions, cause the most mistakes and are best avoided.
articles.one-liner: Nielsen Norman Group research shows that users equate accordion icons with specific behaviors, with carets serving as the most intuitive choice.

summary.what: Research by NN/g indicates that carets are the most performant and intuitive icons for accordions. Using no icon often confuses users, who may mistakenly expect a new page to load, while split menus (where the icon and text perform different actions) are a significant usability anti-pattern.
summary.takeaway: Stick to caret icons for your accordions to align with user expectations, and avoid split-trigger designs to minimize user error.

articles.deep-summary:
* Carets are the preferred standard for accordions.
* Plus icons are acceptable but slightly less effective than carets for indicating expand/collapse.
* Accordions without icons lead users to expect a navigation change (new page) rather than an inline expansion.
* Split menus where the icon and label perform separate actions (e.g., expanding vs. opening the page) are highly error-prone.
* Accordions should be consistently marked with clear affordances to signal expandability.
articles.decoder:
* **Accordion**: A UI pattern that allows users to toggle between hiding and showing large amounts of content in a small space.
* **Affordance**: A visual cue that informs a user how they can interact with an element.

articles.title: Why AI Projects Often Fall Short of Expectations: Insights from a PowerGate Software Expert
articles.description: AI projects usually disappoint for reasons unrelated to the model: the wrong use case, scattered data, and tools that never connect to existing workflows.
articles.one-liner: AI projects frequently fail because organizations prioritize the technology over specific business problems, fragmented data, and existing operational workflows.

summary.what: Chung Tran of PowerGate Software notes that successful AI implementations require aligning tools with clear business objectives rather than treating them as separate applications. IBM research echoes these findings, citing data quality, governance, and workflow integration as primary hurdles beyond the AI model itself.
summary.why: The industry is shifting from an experimental 'AI-first' phase to an 'execution-first' phase where the focus returns to fundamental operational constraints rather than just model performance.
summary.takeaway: Before purchasing or building AI tools, audit your internal data quality and map out the exact manual process you intend to replace to ensure a measurable ROI.

articles.deep-summary:
* Prioritize solving a specific business problem rather than deploying a tool for the sake of adoption.
* Audit data readiness; fragmented or inconsistent data limits model effectiveness more than model architecture.
* Redesign existing workflows to accommodate AI touchpoints, as software rarely plugs into legacy processes seamlessly.
* Define success metrics beyond technical ones (e.g., latency, accuracy) by focusing on business impact like cost reduction or task cycle times.
* Start small with focused use cases to gather feedback and refine the model before scaling.
* Expect ongoing maintenance costs and monitoring; AI is not a set-and-forget implementation.
articles.decoder:
* **CRM (Customer Relationship Management)**: Software used to manage interactions with customers and potential leads.
* **ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning)**: Software that manages core business processes like accounting, supply chain, and procurement.
